name: United Way (US network, charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: the US United Way network.
summary: The US United Way network (about 1,100 local United Ways and their national office, United Way Worldwide) raises money, mostly through workplace campaigns, and spends it on grants to local agencies (about 58% of its programme spending), the 211 helplines it runs or funds, free tax filing and programmes of its own. All of it is modelled, for the network's fiscal year to June 2025 ($3.5 billion spent), in five branches: basic-needs grants valued near cash; other grants and United Way's own services (about 80% of programme spending, including the cost of running the grants) built from the US research on programmes of their kind, children's tutoring, mentoring and early learning valued by the adult earnings the trials imply, job training and coaching by earnings gained, health services at what low-income recipients would pay for them; 211 by the help callers find that they wouldn't have found otherwise; and tax help by fees saved and credits that would have gone unclaimed. Every branch is discounted for missing data, since United Way measures none of these outcomes itself. The result, about 0.010 years of healthy life per $1,000 (0.0007 to 0.14), is under a three-hundredth of the median global-health charity on the site because the help goes to people in the US who consume around $41,000 a year: on the site's log-income scale a dollar does about a sixtieth of what it does for a household living on about $2 a day, and United Way's money buys services at US prices. About four-fifths of the result is the children's and youth programmes' lifelong earnings, so the discount rate, what a child's place in such a programme costs and how much it raises later earnings drive it, with the missing-data and income-to-health sliders.

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: What the modelled program cost in the year the outcomes below are counted for, including its share of overhead. From audited financial statements or the annual report.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: How many people, animals or meals the spending reached in the same year, as the charity reports it.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: What the intervention does for each unit reached, from the best available studies, before any adjustment.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, and delivery falling short. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction, tonnes of CO₂e, chicken pain days) and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: The outcome in the family's shared unit, per dollar.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

output.label: Years of healthy life per dollar you give

rows.label: Programme spending of the US United Way network (grants, 211, free tax help and its own programmes), fiscal year to June 2025
rows.explainer: Every programme the network runs is modelled, so this is all of its programme spending, split below into five branches (Convention 4): grants for basic needs (bn), other grants (og), 211, free tax help (tax) and United Way's other own programmes (own). The year is the network's, as Forbes compiles it from the local United Ways' reports (fiscal year ending 30 June 2025); 211 and tax counts are the nearest published years (2024, 2023), and prices are left in the year they were reported (the half-year gap moves the result by about 1%).

rows.label: Total expenses of the US United Way network, fiscal year to June 2025

source.title: Forbes, America's Top Charities: United Way Worldwide (data as of December 2025, fiscal year ending 30 June 2025)

rows.explainer: The network's total spending, as Forbes compiles it for 'the umbrella for more than 1,100 independent units' (each local United Way files its own audited accounts; United Way Worldwide's audited statements, $77.4 million in 2024, cover only the national office, funded by the locals' dues). Forbes warns its results 'may be skewed due to unconsolidated data'; the uncertainty is carried by the programme share (program_expenses), since the result is per dollar and the total enters only through the overhead ratio. The range, $3.4 to $3.6 billion, is Forbes's rounding to the nearest $0.1 billion.

rows.label: Charitable services (programme expenses) of the US United Way network, fiscal year to June 2025

source.title: Forbes, America's Top Charities: United Way Worldwide (data as of December 2025, fiscal year ending 30 June 2025)

rows.explainer: Forbes's 'charitable services', $2.9 billion of $3.5 billion (84%; management and general $267 million, fundraising $288 million). The range is the programme ratio of two large local United Ways' audited accounts and a little above Forbes's: Greater Twin Cities 77% (2024, $2.7 billion at that ratio), Greater Houston 83% (fiscal year to March 2024), up to 84.3%.

rows.label: Overhead multiplier (total ÷ program expenses)
rows.explainer: Spreads management and fundraising over programs in proportion to their cost, as GiveWell and ACE do.

rows.label: Cost of the modelled program, including overhead
Share of programme spending that is grants to local partner agencies

source.title: United Way of Greater Houston, financial statements, years ended March 31, 2024 and 2023 (Blazek & Vetterling); Greater Twin Cities United Way, financial statements 2024
source.quote: Community investments (grants for program services) $ 35,341,238 (Houston; programme services $51,785,116). Twin Cities: grants to nonprofits for programs $15,376,729, services provided by Greater Twin Cities United Way $17,488,780.

rows.explainer: No network-wide split is published; two large local United Ways' audited statements are the anchors: Greater Houston 68% of programme spending as grants, Greater Twin Cities 47% (https://www.gtcuw.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/GTCUW-Financial-Statements-2024.pdf). The midpoint is the best guess, the two the range.

rows.label: Grants to local partner agencies
rows.explainer: About $1.7 billion a year to the community agencies United Way funds (29,000 worldwide, United Way's count: 'we partnered with 35,000 companies ... and 29,000 community agencies', https://unitedway.org/sites/default/files/2024-10/UWW_overview_8-24.pdf).

rows.label: Share of the grants for basic needs (food, shelter, rent and utility help, emergency aid)
rows.explainer: Our judgment; United Way publishes no national split of its grants, and local United Ways use different impact areas (health, education or youth, financial stability, basic needs). Housing, utilities and food lead what people ask 211 for (47% of 2024 referrals were for housing and utilities), and anchors from local reports: Tulsa Area United Way's 2025 report puts 14% of its investments in community resiliency (https://issuu.com/tauwmarketing/docs/2025_tauw_annual_report), the only published numeric split we found. United Way of Greater Cincinnati's $37.2 million in 2024 goes to three areas, one of them housing security, without a split (https://www.uwgc.org/?p=16767). 211's requests (47% housing and utilities) show where the need is and pull grants toward basic needs. 25%, from Tulsa's 14% to 45%.

rows.label: Grants for basic needs
Other grants (education, early learning and child care, youth, health, financial stability)
United Way Worldwide (the national office) total expenses, 2024 (context)

source.title: United Way Worldwide and Subsidiaries, consolidated financial statements, December 31, 2024 and 2023 (Grant Thornton, 30 May 2025)

rows.explainer: Context only, not used in the result: the national office (brand, network support, donor-advised giving, training), funded largely by the locals' membership dues ($28.8 million in 2024). About 2% of the network's spending and part of its cost through those dues; a gift to United Way Worldwide itself is valued here as the network's average dollar.

rows.label: People the United Way network says it serves each year

source.title: United Way Worldwide and Subsidiaries, consolidated financial statements, December 31, 2024 and 2023 (Grant Thornton, 30 May 2025)
source.quote: It impacts more than 48 million people every year through programs and initiatives that advance health, youth opportunity, financial security, and community resilience.

rows.explainer: United Way's own count, worldwide, all programmes, with duplicates. It sets only how thinly the grants and programmes are spread (on the log scale a dollar spread over more people is worth very slightly more), not their total value, which comes from the spending.

rows.label: Share of those people reached through grants and United Way's own programmes in the US
rows.explainer: Our judgment: the 48 million include Canada (United Way Centraide Canada counts 7.3 million) and other countries, and 211 callers (16.8 million US requests in 2024, perhaps 10 million people). What is left for US grants and programmes is about 28 to 35 million, 60% to 70%; from 40% (more duplication) to 80%. It barely moves the result.

rows.label: Households reached by grants and United Way's own programmes
rows.explainer: United Way counts people, not households: the people reached over the US household size.

rows.label: People per household
rows.explainer: The site's US household size (@household_size.united_states, BLS). Food, rent and utility help, tax refunds and 211's help reach the whole household.

rows.label: People reached by grants and United Way's own programmes (shared by the bn, og and own branches)
Cost per person reached
rows.explainer: Context: about $120 of spending per person counted, with overhead; the services are many and small (a pantry visit, weeks of child care, a tax return).

rows.label: 211 requests for help in the US, 2024 (calls, texts and chats)

source.title: United Way Worldwide, 'Calls for help jumped 1.4M during 2024' (211 2024 Impact Survey)
source.quote: The 16.8 million calls averaged to 32 calls, texts, or online chats per minute.

rows.explainer: Requests to the 211 helplines, which connect callers to local help. 'Nearly 200 call centers across the country, 80% of which are operated or funded in part by local United Way organizations'.

rows.label: Revenue of the 211 network, all funders, 2022

source.title: 211, 2022 Annual Impact Survey (national 211 network, 240 organisations; hosted by NJ 211)

rows.explainer: What all 211 centres together took in, from every funder, in 2022: the best measure of what 211 costs.

rows.label: 211 requests for help, 2022
rows.explainer: Requests in the same year as the revenue (2022 counted requests more broadly than 2024's 16.8 million calls, texts and chats, so the cost per request is if anything low).

rows.label: Cost of a 211 request (all funders), 2024 prices
rows.explainer: The network's 2022 revenue over its 2022 requests ($13.90), in 2024 prices (Convention 8): about $15. A Knoxville 211 put its cost at $3.50 a call and said most centres run three to four times that (NACo, https://naco.org/articles/211-keeps-county-residents-connected-social-services), which agrees.

rows.label: Share of 211's cost paid by United Ways
rows.explainer: Our judgment: 80% of the centres are operated or funded in part by United Ways, but states, counties, health systems and federal contracts pay much of the cost (Greater Houston's 211 Texas line runs largely on a state contract). Half, from 30% to 75%.

rows.label: United Way spending on 211
rows.explainer: About $125 million, 4% of the network's programme spending.

rows.label: People in the households 211 helped connect
rows.explainer: Each request counted as one household's (repeat callers make it an upper bound, which matters only through the log scale).

rows.label: Tax returns prepared free at United Way-supported VITA sites in a year

source.title: United Way, 'United Way and MyFreeTaxes' and 'IRS Volunteer Income Tax Assistance Program (VITA)' (two-page fact sheet, 2023-24)
source.quote: With United Way's help, more than 3,200 VITA sites prepared almost 1 million tax returns last year -- generating $1.8 billion in refunds to low- and moderate-income households in local communities across America.

rows.explainer: United Way's count for the 2023 filing season ('almost 1 million'); the low end allows for sites United Ways support only in part. Free tax filing is the largest of United Way's own programmes with published outcomes; its own branch (Convention 4).

rows.label: Refunds on those returns

source.title: United Way, 'United Way and MyFreeTaxes' and 'IRS Volunteer Income Tax Assistance Program (VITA)' (two-page fact sheet, 2023-24)
source.quote: generating $1.8 billion in refunds to low- and moderate-income households

rows.explainer: Refunds, mostly the Earned Income and Child Tax Credits; most would have been claimed anyway (tax_unclaimed_share).

rows.label: Filing fee saved per return

source.title: United Way, 'United Way and MyFreeTaxes' and 'IRS Volunteer Income Tax Assistance Program (VITA)' (two-page fact sheet, 2023-24)
source.quote: Since 2009, MyFreeTaxes has helped low-to-moderate income filers complete 1.3 million federal returns. This has resulted in savings of $260 million in filing fees and $2 billion in refunds.

rows.explainer: $260 million over 1.3 million returns: $200 a return, United Way's figure for what a paid preparer would have charged; from $150 to $300 (paid preparers' fees for credit claimants vary widely).

rows.label: United Way's spending per free return (site coordination, outreach, MyFreeTaxes)
rows.explainer: Our judgment; the network doesn't publish its tax-programme spending. The returns are prepared by volunteers; United Ways pay for coordinators, sites, training and outreach, and about 100 of them hold IRS VITA grants (federal money, not counted as United Way's). $40 a return (about $40 million in all), from $20 to $100.

rows.label: United Way spending on free tax help
People in the households filing
United Way's other own programme spending (early learning, reading, financial coaching, community schools, grantmaking work)
Share of that spending that is services delivered to people
rows.explainer: Our judgment, anchored on the one published split. Greater Twin Cities United Way's note 15 (Financial Statements 2024, https://www.gtcuw.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/GTCUW-Financial-Statements-2024.pdf) splits its $17.5 million of services provided directly: community impact strategy and grants management $4.24 million, 211 $3.84 million (a branch of its own here), the 988 suicide line $2.88 million, Volunteer United $0.58 million, goal-area programmes $5.42 million, capacity building and other $0.54 million. Of the goal-area lines, Generation Next ($1.34 million, a collective-impact partnership) and the Start Early Funders Coalition ($0.16 million) are convening, not services. Without 211, direct services to people (988 and the other goal-area programmes: food, housing, Action Day, career academies, early childhood; $6.80 million) are 50% of $13.66 million; grants management, convening, volunteering and capacity building, whose value is in the grants, are cost here. 50%, from 35% (more grantmaking and convening elsewhere; Greater Houston doesn't split its own) to 75%.

rows.label: United Way's own services to people (other than 211 and tax help)
Life satisfaction gained per person per year (not counted: valued as income)
rows.explainer: 0 by construction, so no range: there is no wellbeing evidence for this mix of services, and its good (food, rent and utility help, child care, tax refunds) is counted as what the help is worth to the people who get it, as income. A wellbeing gain as well would count the same relief twice (the family's rule: one measure per change).

rows.label: Years the wellbeing effect lasts
rows.explainer: Not used, since the wellbeing branch is 0 by construction (ls_gain_per_person_year); the template's range is kept so the row reads as in every model of the family, from half a year to three years for a service's wellbeing effect.

rows.label: WELLBYs per person reached, discounted
rows.explainer: Point-years, discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Share of a grantee agency's spending that reaches clients as services
rows.explainer: Our judgment: a grant pays for the agency's overhead too. Programme ratios of US human-service charities are typically 75% to 90% (United Way's own network: 84%); 82%. It reduces the basic-needs grants to what reaches clients, and grosses United Way's own programme-only spending up to the full-cost basis of the trialled programmes' costs (own_uov_raw), since United Way's own overhead is already in overhead_ratio.

rows.label: Basic needs: what a dollar of food, rent or utility help is worth to the household against cash
rows.explainer: Our judgment: food, rent and utility help frees money the household would spend on the same things, so it is close to cash; the gap is for help that isn't the household's own top need. Food aid within what a household buys anyway is valued near cash (the usual finding for SNAP); 0.9, from 0.7 to 1.

rows.label: Basic needs: value per person reached
Value per person reached (basic-needs grants; the other branches are valued per participant)
rows.explainer: The basic-needs grants' cash-equivalent value spread over the people reached, for reading against other domestic-services models; the other grants and own services are valued per participant from the literature, 211 and tax help per contact and per return.

rows.label: Average consumption per person in the country (US$)
rows.explainer: The site's US consumption per person, 2024 (@united_states.consumption_per_person_2024, World Bank), scaled to the clients by recipients_consumption_share.

rows.label: Anchor: consumption per person of the poorest fifth of US households, as a share of the average person's
rows.explainer: Context: the poorest fifth spend 45% of the average household's (BLS 2024), in households of 1.6 people against 2.4: per person 0.67 of the average.

rows.label: The people served's consumption per person, as a share of the average
rows.explainer: The shared poorest-fifth anchor times the clients' judged position relative to it (clients_vs_poorest_fifth).

rows.label: Clients' consumption per person relative to the poorest fifth's
rows.explainer: United Way's grants, 211 and tax help go mostly to households below or near the poverty line ('ALICE' and below, about the poorest 40%): a little above the poorest fifth's 0.67 of the average per person (poorest_fifth_consumption_share), so 1.05 of it (0.7 of the average), from 0.82 (mostly well below the poverty line) to 1.27 (many near-poor and middle-income users of child care, youth and tax programmes).

rows.label: The people served's consumption per person (US$)
Years the help counts as income
rows.explainer: One by construction, so no range: the services are a year's flow, consumed in the year (Convention 3). Lasting effects (a child's school readiness, a family kept housed) are in unmodelled_benefits_adj, not here, so they aren't counted twice.

rows.label: ln(consumption) gain per person reached, all branches (context)
rows.explainer: Context only: every branch's gain before adjustments, over the people reached by grants and own programmes.

rows.label: Basic needs: ln(consumption) gain per person
Other grants and own services: share for children and youth (early learning, reading, tutoring, mentoring, after-school)
rows.explainer: Our judgment: United Way sorts its non-emergency work into education (early learning, grade-level reading, youth), financial stability and health, and publishes no national split. Anchor: United Way of Abilene's 2025 annual report puts its three impact areas at Health $413,000 (26%), Education & Youth Services $544,500 (34%) and Financial Stability $624,835 (40%), the last including the basic-needs help that is a branch of its own here, so education's share of what is left is higher; Greater Houston describes its work as financial stability 'coupled with early childhood and youth development programs and health care programs', and Greater Twin Cities' restricted funds are mostly for 'educational success' and early childhood. 40%, from 25% to 55%.

rows.label: Other grants and own services: share for financial stability (financial coaching, job training, work supports)
rows.explainer: Our judgment, from the same anchors as the children's share (Abilene's Financial Stability 40% including basic needs; United Way of Puerto Rico puts 22% of the funds it raises into financial stability; Greater Houston's THRIVE financial-stability network is its largest restricted fund). 30%, from 15% to 45%. The rest, 1 minus the two shares (30% at the defaults), is health and other services.

rows.label: Children and youth: cost per child of a year of a programme as trialled
rows.explainer: Our judgment, the full cost (the agency's overhead included, so grants are not reduced by agency_programme_share here) of one child's year in a programme of the kind the trials below test, since the trials' effects come with their dose. Anchors: Big Brothers Big Sisters community mentoring about $1,500 to $3,300 per youth (Alfonso and others 2019; the Washington State Institute for Public Policy uses $4,399 per participant a year), high-dosage tutoring about $3,000 to $4,000 per student-year (the Chicago Saga math tutoring trials, about $3,800), state pre-kindergarten several times that. $3,000, from $1,200 to $8,000: lighter-touch programmes cost less but would do less than the trials.

rows.label: Children and youth: effect of a programme year, in standard deviations of the outcomes

source.title: Kraft and others, 'What Impacts Should We Expect From Tutoring at Scale? Exploring Meta-Analytic Generalizability', Review of Educational Research 2026 (published abstract)
source.page: Abstract (the publisher's page blocks automated readers; the abstract is in the Crossref record for the DOI)
source.quote: Pooled effect sizes from studies with stronger target-equivalence are .16 to .22 standard deviations, relative to .40 standard deviations in our full sample.

rows.explainer: The research on programmes of this kind at the scale United Way funds them, weighted by a judged quarter each of its children's spending. Tutoring and reading at scale, 0.19 SD: the midpoint of 0.16 to 0.22 on standardised tests in the published article's large, policy-relevant RCTs (263 trials), against 0.40 in its full sample of mostly small efficacy trials; the earlier working paper (EdWorkingPaper ai24-1031, https://edworkingpapers.com/ai24-1031) puts the at-scale effects at 'only a third to a half as large' as the full sample, 0.13 to 0.20, the same range. Youth mentoring, 0.21: Raposa and others (Journal of Youth and Adolescence 2019), g = 0.21 across outcomes in 70 studies, mean age 12; the Big Brothers Big Sisters community-mentoring RCT finds small positive effects on emotional and conduct outcomes at 13 months (Herrera and others 2023) and, in its four-year report, less violent delinquency and substance use but no significant effect on arrests (DuBois and others, June 2025, https://youthrex.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/YRS-4-Year-Report_062025.pdf). Early learning, 0.15: Head Start's end-of-programme gains in its national RCT, about 0.1 to 0.2 SD on cognitive outcomes, fading on tests later (Puma and others, Head Start Impact Study final report, US HHS 2010). After-school programmes, 0.09: the national evaluation of 21st Century Community Learning Centers found no academic gains (James-Burdumy and others, Mathematica for the US Department of Education, 2005), while Durlak, Weissberg and Pachan's meta-analysis (American Journal of Community Psychology 2010) finds 0.12 on grades and 0.17 on tests (Table 3), with the effects in the programmes using sequenced, active, focused and explicit (SAFE) practices and the rest near zero; 0.09 is between them. (0.19 + 0.21 + 0.15 + 0.09) ÷ 4 = 0.16. The low end, 0.05, is programmes with little effect, 0.30 the high end. Whether United Way's grantees run at the trials' dose is the missing-data step's question, not this row's.

rows.label: Children and youth: adult earnings gain per standard deviation of the childhood gain

source.title: Chetty, Friedman and Rockoff, 'Measuring the Impacts of Teachers II: Teacher Value-Added and Student Outcomes in Adulthood', American Economic Review 2014 (NBER Working Paper 19424, revision 2)
source.quote: On average, a one standard deviation improvement in teacher VA in a single grade raises earnings by 1.3% at age 28.

rows.explainer: A teacher one standard deviation better in value-added raises a year's test scores by about 0.12 SD in maths and 0.08 SD in English (the same authors' summary, 'Great Teaching: Measuring Its Effects on Students' Future Earnings', Education Next 2012, https://www.educationnext.org/great-teaching/) and earnings at 28 by 1.3%: 1.3% ÷ 0.10 SD (the average of maths and English) = about 13% per SD of a one-year test gain, measured in adulthood, so the fade-out of test scores is already in it (in Project STAR too, classroom-quality effects fade on tests and re-emerge in earnings: Chetty and others, Quarterly Journal of Economics 2011). 10%, from 5% to 13%: below CFR's 13% because much of the youth programmes' gain is in social-emotional or self-reported outcomes, which predict earnings less than test gains; this is the only place that doubt is counted.

rows.label: Children and youth: years from the programme to working age
rows.explainer: Our judgment: United Way's youth work runs from early learning (age 3 to 5, 17 to 19 years before work at about 22) to mentoring and after-school programmes (average age about 12 in the mentoring trials, about 10 years). 13 years, from 8 to 18; every year is discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Children and youth: years the earnings gain lasts
rows.explainer: The site's shared figure for how long a childhood programme's earnings gain lasts (GiveWell's, 40 years, from 30), the same as for deworming and malaria prevention.

rows.label: Children and youth: household sharing of the adult's earnings gain
rows.explainer: The site's shared figure for a later-life earnings gain shared with the earner's household (GiveWell's 2, from 1 to 3), as in every model that values a childhood programme's adult income.

rows.label: Children and youth: ln(consumption) gain per child, all working years, discounted
rows.formula: ln(1 + edu_effect_sd * edu_earnings_per_sd) * pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, edu_working_years) / (1 + $discount_rate) ^ edu_years_until_work * edu_resource_sharing
rows.explainer: The proportional earnings gain on the log scale for each working year, discounted to the programme year at the shared rate, shared with the household. A proportional gain is the same on the log scale whatever the adult's income, so the clients' consumption share doesn't enter. Taxes on the gain and benefits lost are not netted out (the site's other income models don't net them either).

rows.label: Financial stability: cost per participant
rows.explainer: Our judgment: financial coaching runs several sessions over months (a few hundred to about $1,500 a client), job training and work-readiness programmes $2,000 to several thousand a participant (WIA intensive services and training, sector programmes more). $2,000, from $700 to $5,000.

rows.label: Financial stability: yearly earnings or savings gain per participant's household
rows.explainer: Our judgment from the trials. Job training and job-search help: average impacts close to zero in the short run, larger 2 to 3 years on and for human-capital programmes (Card, Kluve and Weber, Journal of the European Economic Association 2018, over 200 evaluations); the national WIA Gold Standard RCT found intensive services raised earnings by about $3,300 to $7,100 over 30 months ($1,300 to $2,800 a year) and training added nothing measurable (Fortson and others, Mathematica 2017). Financial coaching: one RCT found higher savings and credit scores at one site and less debt at the other (Theodos and others, Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization 2018), but a systematic review of 11 studies (Birkenmaier and others, Research on Social Work Practice 2026) finds the financial effects mostly small and mixed. Most of United Way's financial-stability money is coaching, benefits access and work supports rather than intensive training: $500 a year, from 0 to $2,500.

rows.label: Financial stability: years the gain lasts
rows.explainer: Our judgment: the training trials' follow-ups run 2 to 5 years with gains persisting or growing (Card, Kluve and Weber 2018); coaching follow-ups are 1 to 2 years. 3 years, from 1 to 5, discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Financial stability: ln(consumption) gain per participant, summed over the household
rows.formula: household_size * ln(1 + fin_earnings_gain / (household_size * baseline_consumption)) * pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, fin_years)
rows.explainer: The household's yearly gain spread over its members at the clients' consumption, for the years it lasts, discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Health and other services: cost per person served
rows.explainer: Our judgment: community clinics, mental-health and substance-use counselling, home care for older people and disability services, from a few visits to a year's care. $800, from $200 to $3,000. On the log scale this matters little: the value per dollar below carries the result.

rows.label: Health and other services: what a dollar of them is worth to low-income recipients, against cash

source.title: Finkelstein, Hendren and Luttmer, 'The Value of Medicaid: Interpreting Results from the Oregon Health Insurance Experiment', Journal of Political Economy 2019 (NBER Working Paper 21308)
source.quote: Our baseline estimates of Medicaid's welfare benefit to recipients per dollar of government spending range from about $0.2 to $0.4, depending on the framework.

rows.explainer: The one randomised measure of what US low-income adults are willing to pay for health care bought for them: $0.20 to $0.40 per dollar of public spending on Medicaid in the Oregon experiment, net of the free care they would otherwise get (more per dollar of net cost, government spending less the roughly $0.6 a dollar that is a transfer to the providers of uncompensated care: the gap is care that would have been given anyway). So this is already net of what would have come anyway. 0.3, from 0.15 to 0.6 (services that substitute for paid help, such as home care or counselling the client would otherwise pay for).

rows.label: Health and other services: ln(consumption) gain per person served, summed over the household
rows.explainer: The service's cash-equivalent value spread over the household at the clients' consumption, in the year it is given.

rows.label: Other grants and own services: ln(consumption) gain per dollar of services
rows.formula: svc_edu_share * edu_ln_gain_per_child / edu_cost_per_child + svc_fin_share * fin_ln_gain_per_participant / fin_cost_per_participant + (1 - svc_edu_share - svc_fin_share) * hlth_ln_gain_per_participant / hlth_cost_per_participant
rows.explainer: Each kind of service's gain per participant over its cost per participant, weighted by its share of the spending. The reach is the spending divided by what the trialled programmes cost: United Way's count of people served doesn't say who got which service.

rows.label: Share of 211 requests that end with the caller getting the help they needed
rows.explainer: Our judgment from follow-up surveys of 211 callers, all self-reported. The national 211 network's 2022 Impact Survey (https://nj211.org/sites/default/files/documents/2023-02/Impact%20Survey%202022.pdf, p. 20): in a six-month follow-up in five markets, mostly of utility requests (51%), '63% were unable to obtain needed help', 37% got it: the low end, since utility funds run out. Requests for food, health and other services, which run out less, do better; the high end, 65%, is our judgment (no published follow-up we could open gives a higher figure). Half, from 37% to 65%.

rows.label: Value of the help a 211 caller obtains, per household
rows.explainer: Our judgment: housing, utilities and food lead the requests (47% of 2024 referrals were housing and utilities); a utility payment is typically a few hundred dollars, a pantry visit under $100, rent help often $1,000 or more but granted to few. $300, from $100 to $800.

rows.label: 211: ln(consumption) gain per person in a helped household
Tax help: share of filers who would otherwise have paid a preparer
rows.explainer: Our judgment: about half of Earned Income Tax Credit claimants use paid preparers (IRS research on EITC returns, often cited at 50% to 60%); the rest of VITA's filers would otherwise use free software or file alone. 50%, from 30% to 70%.

rows.label: Tax help: share of the refunds that wouldn't have been claimed without free help
rows.explainer: Our judgment: most VITA filers would have filed anyway, but some would have missed credits (the IRS puts EITC take-up near 78%, so about a fifth of eligible people don't claim) or filed late. 7% of the refunds, from 2% to 15%.

rows.label: Tax help: value added per return
rows.explainer: Fees saved for those who would have paid, plus credits that would have gone unclaimed: about $230.

rows.label: Tax help: ln(consumption) gain per person in a filing household
Illness averted per person reached, in DALYs (not counted separately)
rows.explainer: 0 by construction, so no range: clinics and health programmes among the grants are valued with the other services, at what they are worth to the people who get them; counting health here as well would count them twice.

rows.label: Deaths averted per person reached (not counted separately)
rows.explainer: 0 by construction, so no range: shelter and rent help may avert some deaths from exposure and overdose among people kept out of homelessness, but there is no network-wide evidence; that possibility is in unmodelled_benefits_adj with homelessness averted. The age split below is kept for the row's shared valuation and doesn't move the result.

rows.label: Share of the deaths averted that are of children under five
rows.explainer: Not used (no deaths are counted); the template's default age split, kept so the row reads the shared value of a death.

rows.label: Of the deaths averted at five or older, share aged 5 to 14
rows.explainer: Not used (no deaths are counted); the template's default age split, kept so the row reads the shared value of a death.

rows.label: Of the deaths averted at 15 or older, share aged 15 to 49
rows.explainer: Not used (no deaths are counted); the template's default age split, kept so the row reads the shared value of a death.

rows.label: Value of a death averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: GiveWell's moral weights by the age band of each death, times your value of a life: the site's one value of a death.

rows.label: Basic needs: units of value before adjustments
Other grants: units of value before adjustments
rows.explainer: The other grants' spending (their agencies' overhead included, as in the trialled programmes' costs) times the literature's gain per dollar, in units of value.

rows.label: United Way's own services: units of value before adjustments
rows.explainer: United Way's own direct services valued at the same literature gain per dollar as the services it funds. The trialled programmes' costs include their providers' overhead, while United Way's own overhead is already in the cost (overhead_ratio): so its programme-only spending is grossed up by the agencies' programme share to the same full-cost basis, not counting its overhead twice.

rows.label: 211: units of value before adjustments
Tax help: units of value before adjustments
Value of a volunteer hour, US, 2025
rows.explainer: The site's US value of a volunteer hour for 2025 (@united_states.volunteer_hour_value_2025, Independent Sector: the average private non-farm wage plus benefits), for tax volunteers' unpaid hours (Convention 2).

rows.label: Basic needs: United Way's share of the resources behind the value counted
rows.explainer: 1: this branch is valued at what United Way's own dollars buy (its spending times what a dollar of the services is worth), so nobody else's resources are in the value counted. Volunteers and co-funders working alongside (United Way counts 1.5 million volunteers) add services that aren't counted here, so they take no share of this value; Convention 2 applies where the value is an outcome several contributors produce, as for 211 and tax help.

rows.label: Other grants: United Way's share of the resources behind the value counted
rows.explainer: 1: this branch is valued at what United Way's own dollars buy (its spending times what a dollar of the services is worth), so nobody else's resources are in the value counted. Volunteers and co-funders working alongside (United Way counts 1.5 million volunteers) add services that aren't counted here, so they take no share of this value; Convention 2 applies where the value is an outcome several contributors produce, as for 211 and tax help.

rows.label: Own services: United Way's share of the resources behind the value counted
rows.explainer: 1: this branch is valued at what United Way's own dollars buy (its spending times what a dollar of the services is worth), so nobody else's resources are in the value counted. Volunteers and co-funders working alongside (United Way counts 1.5 million volunteers) add services that aren't counted here, so they take no share of this value; Convention 2 applies where the value is an outcome several contributors produce, as for 211 and tax help.

rows.label: Basic needs: share of the help that wouldn't have come anyway from government or family
rows.explainer: Our judgment: without the help some households would get the same from government programmes, other charities or family. Emergency help is rationed: in Evans, Sullivan and Wallskog (Science 2016), Chicago callers who asked for rent help when funds had run out were much more likely to enter a homeless shelter than those helped, so turned-away people often find nothing. 80%, from 60% to 95%. Whether the agency would have given the help anyway with other donors' money is bn_leverage_funging_adj.

rows.label: Other grants: share of the outcome that wouldn't have come anyway
rows.explainer: 1: the trials' effects are already net of what their control groups got elsewhere (public pre-K, school programmes, other charities), and the health value is net of the free care recipients would get anyway (Finkelstein, Hendren and Luttmer). Whether the agency would have run the service with other money is og_leverage_funging_adj.

rows.label: Own services: share of the outcome that wouldn't have come anyway
rows.explainer: 1, as for the other grants: the trial effects are net of the control groups' other services. Whether partners would run the programmes without United Way is own_leverage_funging_adj.

rows.label: Basic needs: evidence adjustment (targeting and validity)
rows.explainer: Our judgment, validity only (delivery is implementation_adj, targeting is in bn_inkind_factor and recipients_consumption_share): food, rent and utility help is valued at its near-cash worth, which rests on prices, and the study evidence for the main kind (Evans et al. 2016: emergency rent help cut shelter entry) supports it doing what it says. 1, down to 0.85 if agencies report more help than they give.

rows.label: Other grants: evidence adjustment (validity of the literature chain)
rows.explainer: Our judgment on the internal validity of the literature chain only. Publication bias and self-report in the mentoring evidence (Raposa and others 2019 find larger effects where evaluations rely on youth self-report); tutoring at scale is taken near face value, since Kraft and others' at-scale figure comes from large RCTs on independent tests, where publication bias is small. Two other doubts are counted elsewhere, once each: that social-emotional gains predict earnings less than test gains (edu_earnings_per_sd), and whether United Way's grantees run programmes like the trialled ones, at their dose (the missing-data step, og_missing_data_adj). 0.85, from 0.65 to 1.

rows.label: Own services: evidence adjustment (as the other grants)
rows.explainer: The same literature chain as the other grants, so the same adjustment.

rows.label: 211: evidence adjustment (self-reported follow-up surveys)
rows.explainer: Our judgment: the help-obtained share comes from self-reported follow-ups that reach only some callers, and those who answer are likelier to have been helped. 0.8, from 0.6 to 1.

rows.label: 211: share of the help callers wouldn't have found without 211
rows.explainer: Our judgment: many callers would find the same help by searching, from a caseworker or by calling the agency; 211's value is the share it adds. No trial measures it. 30%, from 10% to 50%.

rows.label: 211: United Way's share of the resources behind the help found
rows.formula: h211_cost_per_contact * h211_uw_cost_share / (h211_cost_per_contact + h211_help_obtained_share * h211_counterfactual_adj * h211_value_of_help / (agency_programme_share * bn_inkind_factor))
rows.explainer: Convention 2: the help a caller finds is paid for by the agency that gives it (often a United Way grantee, counted in the grants), so 211 is credited with United Way's part of the contact's cost over the contact's cost plus the cost of the help it added (the help's value over what a dollar of basic-needs grants is worth). About 10%.

rows.label: Tax help: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: Our judgment on the figures' validity: returns and refunds are United Way's counts and the fee is its figure. The counterfactual shares are judgments, which the missing-data step (tax_missing_data_adj) counts, so they aren't discounted here again. 1, down to 0.8 for preparation errors and refunds counted twice across VITA and MyFreeTaxes.

rows.label: Tax help: volunteer hours per return
rows.explainer: Our judgment: an IRS-certified volunteer prepares a typical credit return in about an hour, plus quality review and intake; with training time spread over a season, about 2 hours a return, from 1 to 4.

rows.label: Tax help: IRS VITA grant money per return
rows.explainer: Our judgment: the IRS funds VITA sites with matching grants (about 100 United Ways hold them, United Way's fact sheet), federal money that is not United Way's; the IRS awarded about $40 million in VITA grants to some 300 organisations for the 2024 season (IRS news release IR-23-191, https://www.irs.gov/newsroom/irs-awards-more-than-40-million-in-grants-for-free-tax-preparation-for-the-2024-filing-season). If United Way grantees hold about a third of it, about $13 million over 950,000 returns, roughly $15 a return; from $8 to $36 (all of it on United Way's returns).

rows.label: Tax help: United Way's share of the resources behind the returns
rows.explainer: Convention 2: United Way's spending per return over that plus the volunteers' hours at the US value of a volunteer hour and the IRS's grant money (about 30%).

rows.label: Tax help: share that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 1: the counterfactual is already in the value per return, which counts only fees that would have been paid and credits that would have gone unclaimed.

rows.label: Share of reported reach that gets the service as described
rows.explainer: 1: the value counted comes from the spending, not from United Way's count of people, so duplicated or over-counted people don't inflate it; delivery shortfalls are in the agency share, the in-kind factor and the trialled programmes' cost per participant. The low end, 0.9, allows for money reported as spent that reached clients late or not at all.

rows.label: Leverage: grants matched by other funders or that unlock public money
rows.explainer: Our judgment, leverage only (funging is in each branch's leverage-and-funging row): some grants are matched by other funders or unlock public money. 1, up to 1.05.

rows.label: Basic needs: share of the grant-funded help the agency wouldn't have given anyway
rows.explainer: Our judgment: agencies replace part of a lost United Way grant from other donors. United Way is usually one funder among several and below the template's 0.95, since its grants are general operating money that other donors can more easily make up. How the anchors lead to 0.85: Andreoni and Payne (Journal of Public Economics 2011) find a government grant cuts a charity's private giving by about 75 cents on the dollar, mostly because the charity then fundraises less. Read in reverse, an agency that loses a grant can raise part of it back, but only by fundraising harder, over time and at a cost; If 75 cents of a lost dollar could come back, the floor would be 25%; the low end sits above it, at 60%, because the replacement money costs the agency fundraising and comes from donors who would otherwise give to charities doing similar good. United Way grants are general operating money, which other donors make up more easily than restricted grants, so the best guess sits below the template's 0.95 for domestic services, at 0.85; the American Red Cross model has 0.95 and GiveWell's top charities typically 0.85 to 0.95. 85%, from 60% to 100%.

rows.label: Other grants: share of the services the agency wouldn't have run anyway
rows.explainer: Our judgment, as for basic needs: United Way is one funder of the agency's programme among several, and agencies make up part of a lost grant. How the anchors lead to 0.85: Andreoni and Payne (Journal of Public Economics 2011) find a government grant cuts a charity's private giving by about 75 cents on the dollar, mostly because the charity then fundraises less. Read in reverse, an agency that loses a grant can raise part of it back, but only by fundraising harder, over time and at a cost; If 75 cents of a lost dollar could come back, the floor would be 25%; the low end sits above it, at 50%, because the replacement money costs the agency fundraising and comes from donors who would otherwise give to charities doing similar good. United Way grants are general operating money, which other donors make up more easily than restricted grants, so the best guess sits below the template's 0.95 for domestic services, at 0.85; the American Red Cross model has 0.95 and GiveWell's top charities typically 0.85 to 0.95. 85%, from 50% to 100%.

rows.label: Own services: share that wouldn't have run without United Way
rows.explainer: Our judgment: United Way's own programmes (early-learning and reading initiatives, the 988 line, coaching) are its own, but partners and public money would take over some of them; nearer the template's default than the grants. 90%, from 70% to 100%.

rows.label: Basic needs: leverage and funging
Other grants: leverage and funging
Own services: leverage and funging
211: leverage and funging
rows.explainer: Leverage only: funging is already in 211's attribution, which credits United Way only its share of the cost of finding help.

rows.label: Tax help: leverage and funging
rows.explainer: Leverage only: the volunteers' and IRS's shares are in the attribution, and filers' alternatives in the counterfactual shares.

rows.label: Leverage and funging (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.formula: (bn_uov_raw * bn_leverage_funging_adj + og_uov_raw * og_leverage_funging_adj + own_uov_raw * own_leverage_funging_adj + tax_uov_raw * tax_leverage_funging_adj + h211_uov_raw * h211_leverage_funging_adj) / (bn_uov_raw + og_uov_raw + own_uov_raw + tax_uov_raw + h211_uov_raw)
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only (Convention 4); each branch applies its own.

rows.label: Basic-needs grants: missing-data step
rows.explainer: Basic-needs grants: thin. United Way publishes neither who got the help nor how much (the basic-needs share of grants and the people reached are judgments), and the value is the help's cost against cash, not a measured effect. So it counts at the shared slider (templates.md Convention 12).

rows.label: Other grants: missing-data step
rows.explainer: Other grants: thin. The effect is the research literature's on programmes of the same kind (tutoring, mentoring, pre-K, job training, coaching, Medicaid), not a measurement of the agencies United Way funds, and who got which service is a judgment. So it counts at the shared slider (templates.md Convention 12).

rows.label: Own services: missing-data step
rows.explainer: Own services: thin, as the other grants: the literature's effects, not United Way's own evaluation of its programmes. So it counts at the shared slider (templates.md Convention 12).

rows.label: 211: missing-data step
rows.explainer: 211: thin. The contacts are counted, but whether callers got help comes from self-reported follow-ups without a comparison group, and what 211 added is a judgment. So it counts at the shared slider (templates.md Convention 12).

rows.label: Tax help: missing-data step
rows.explainer: Tax help: thin. The returns and refunds are United Way's counts, but whether filers would have paid a preparer or missed credits is a judgment, not a measured counterfactual. So it counts at the shared slider (templates.md Convention 12).

rows.label: Missing-data step (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.formula: (bn_uov_raw * bn_missing_data_adj + og_uov_raw * og_missing_data_adj + own_uov_raw * own_missing_data_adj + tax_uov_raw * tax_missing_data_adj + h211_uov_raw * h211_missing_data_adj) / (bn_uov_raw + og_uov_raw + own_uov_raw + tax_uov_raw + h211_uov_raw)
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only (Convention 4); every branch is thin, so each applies the shared slider.

rows.label: Basic needs: all adjustments
rows.formula: bn_evidence_adj * bn_counterfactual_adj * bn_attribution_share * implementation_adj * bn_leverage_funging_adj * bn_missing_data_adj

rows.label: Other grants: all adjustments
rows.formula: og_evidence_adj * og_counterfactual_adj * og_attribution_share * implementation_adj * og_leverage_funging_adj * og_missing_data_adj

rows.label: Own services: all adjustments
rows.formula: own_evidence_adj * own_counterfactual_adj * own_attribution_share * implementation_adj * own_leverage_funging_adj * own_missing_data_adj

rows.label: Tax help: all adjustments
rows.formula: tax_evidence_adj * tax_counterfactual_adj * tax_attribution_share * implementation_adj * tax_leverage_funging_adj * tax_missing_data_adj

rows.label: 211: all adjustments
rows.formula: h211_evidence_adj * h211_counterfactual_adj * h211_attribution_share * implementation_adj * h211_leverage_funging_adj * h211_missing_data_adj

rows.label: Evidence adjustment (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only (Convention 4); each branch applies its own.
rows.formula: (bn_uov_raw * bn_evidence_adj + og_uov_raw * og_evidence_adj + own_uov_raw * own_evidence_adj + tax_uov_raw * tax_evidence_adj + h211_uov_raw * h211_evidence_adj) / (bn_uov_raw + og_uov_raw + own_uov_raw + tax_uov_raw + h211_uov_raw)

rows.label: Counterfactual adjustment (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only (Convention 4); each branch applies its own.
rows.formula: (bn_uov_raw * bn_counterfactual_adj + og_uov_raw * og_counterfactual_adj + own_uov_raw * own_counterfactual_adj + tax_uov_raw * tax_counterfactual_adj + h211_uov_raw * h211_counterfactual_adj) / (bn_uov_raw + og_uov_raw + own_uov_raw + tax_uov_raw + h211_uov_raw)

rows.label: United Way's share of the resources behind the outcome (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only (Convention 4); each branch applies its own.
rows.formula: (bn_uov_raw * bn_attribution_share + og_uov_raw * og_attribution_share + own_uov_raw * own_attribution_share + tax_uov_raw * tax_attribution_share + h211_uov_raw * h211_attribution_share) / (bn_uov_raw + og_uov_raw + own_uov_raw + tax_uov_raw + h211_uov_raw)

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only (Convention 4); each branch applies its own.

rows.label: All adjustments (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.formula: (bn_uov_raw * bn_total_adj + og_uov_raw * og_total_adj + own_uov_raw * own_total_adj + tax_uov_raw * tax_total_adj + h211_uov_raw * h211_total_adj) / (bn_uov_raw + og_uov_raw + own_uov_raw + tax_uov_raw + h211_uov_raw)
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only (Convention 4); each branch applies its own.

rows.label: Benefits and harms not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Our judgment, effects not modelled, each with its sign: homelessness averted by rent help beyond the money (Evans, Sullivan and Wallskog, Science 2016) and any deaths it averts (+); youth programmes' effects on crime and teen births beyond earnings (+; the earnings are modelled); public-policy work for tax credits and 211 (+); the national office's administration of FEMA's Emergency Food and Shelter Program as fiscal agent (+, small); grants that keep weak agencies going out of habit (−). +5%, from −5% to +20%.

rows.label: Income and deaths, in units of value, after each branch's adjustments
rows.formula: bn_uov_raw * bn_total_adj + og_uov_raw * og_total_adj + own_uov_raw * own_total_adj + tax_uov_raw * tax_total_adj + h211_uov_raw * h211_total_adj + people_reached * deaths_averted_per_person * value_per_death * bn_total_adj

rows.explainer: The bridge from UoV into healthy years (docs/normalization.md 2.6): fixed, don't edit.

Life satisfaction gained, in healthy years
rows.explainer: The bridge from WELLBYs into healthy years (docs/normalization.md 2.6): fixed, don't edit.

Years of healthy life
rows.explainer: Every outcome in healthy years, each branch already adjusted (Convention 4), times the share for effects not modelled.

rows.label: Years of healthy life per dollar
Staff pay as a share of total expenses
rows.explainer: Our judgment anchored on two large local United Ways' accounts: salaries and benefits over total expenses, Greater Houston 28% ($17.7 million of $62.5 million, https://unitedwayhouston.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/09/United-Way-of-Greater-Houston-2024-FS-SA.pdf) and Greater Twin Cities 45% ($19.0 million of $42.6 million, https://www.gtcuw.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/GTCUW-Financial-Statements-2024.pdf, which passes fewer grants through its expenses). 35%, between them. Grantee agencies' staff are theirs, not United Way's.

rows.label: Pay gap versus comparable jobs elsewhere
rows.explainer: The shared pay gap for staff hired locally (@staff_pay.gap_local_delivery): United Way's staff are paid near local nonprofit rates.

Share of the full cost paid by cash donations
